questions.stem: What is the primary function of the respiratory system?
questions.why: The primary function is bringing oxygen in and eliminating carbon dioxide. Nonspecific defense, pH control, and vocalization are secondary.

options.t: Warming and humidifying the air you breathe
options.why: That is a function of the upper airway, not the whole system.

options.t: Producing speech and protecting the airway
options.why: Both are secondary functions rather than the primary one.

options.t: Regulating blood pressure and fluid volume
options.why: Those are cardiovascular and renal roles.

options.t: Taking in oxygen and eliminating carbon dioxide

questions.stem: Where does gas exchange actually take place?
questions.why: The four parts are the respiratory tract, the respiratory membrane where gas exchange happens, the lungs, and the diaphragm with the chest wall and accessory muscles.

options.why: The diaphragm drives ventilation mechanically.
The tract is the set of passages moving air, not the exchange surface.
The pleural space is a potential space around the lungs.

questions.stem: What separates the upper airway from the lower airway?
questions.why: The airway divides at the glottis — the vocal cords and the opening between them. Above it lies the head and neck; below it, the chest.

options.why: The epiglottis is the flap forming the glottis's upper border.
The carina is where the trachea splits, well below the divide.
The cricoid is a cartilage, not the dividing landmark.

questions.stem: What are the major functions of the upper airway?
questions.why: The upper airway warms, filters, and humidifies air entering through the nose and mouth on its way to the trachea.

options.why: Exchange occurs at the alveoli in the lower airway.

options.t: Generating the pressure that moves air
options.why: Pressure changes come from the diaphragm and chest wall.
That is the job of the chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: Which three regions make up the pharynx?
questions.why: The pharynx sits between the nasal cavity and the larynx and consists of the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.

options.why: Those are laryngeal structures.
Hypopharynx is not the term used here.
Those are neighbouring structures, not pharyngeal regions.

questions.stem: What do the turbinates do?
questions.why: Turbinates are three curved bone shelves in each nasal passage. They create turbulence so inhaled particles stick to the walls, and with the vascular supply they warm, filter, and humidify air.

options.why: They shape airflow rather than provide structural support.
That is the job of the ciliated mucous lining.
That is the soft palate's role.

questions.stem: What happens to the soft palate during swallowing?
questions.why: Muscles elevate the soft palate until it touches the posterior pharyngeal wall, sealing the nasopharynx from the oropharynx — which keeps food out of the nose.

options.t: It drops to open the airway wider
options.why: It elevates rather than drops.

options.t: It tightens to open the eustachian tube
options.why: Eustachian tube opening is a separate pressure-equalizing action.

options.t: It closes the glottis against aspiration
options.why: The epiglottis protects the glottis.

options.t: It rises and seals off the nasopharynx

questions.stem: What forms the nasal septum?
questions.why: The nasal septum divides the nasopharynx into two passages and is composed of the ethmoid and vomer bones plus cartilage.

options.why: The sphenoid sits behind the nasal cavity.
Bone makes up most of the septum.
Those bones form the palate rather than the septum.

options.t: Ethmoid and vomer bones plus cartilage

questions.stem: What is the function of the eustachian tubes?
questions.why: The eustachian (auditory) tubes run from the inner ear, allowing fluid drainage and equalization of pressure behind the tympanic membrane.

options.t: Draining fluid and equalizing ear pressure
Draining the frontal and maxillary sinuses
options.why: Sinus drainage happens through separate openings.

options.t: Connecting the nasopharynx to the trachea
options.why: The trachea connects below the larynx.

options.t: Carrying olfactory signals to the brain
options.why: Smell travels via the olfactory nerves.

questions.stem: What passes through the oropharynx that does not pass through the nasopharynx?
questions.why: The nasopharynx carries air only; the oropharynx is a passageway for both air and food, running from the soft palate down to the epiglottis.

options.why: Air passes through both regions.
Sinus drainage enters the nasal cavity above.
Exhaled gas travels the same route as inhaled air.

questions.stem: Stimulating the posterior pharynx triggers which reflex?
questions.why: The posterior pharynx is richly supplied with sensitive nerves. Stimulation triggers the gag reflex, which produces coughing or retching to prevent aspiration.

options.why: Coughing is one component of gagging, not the reflex name.
Hering-Breuer prevents lung overinflation.
Micturition is a bladder reflex.

questions.stem: The laryngopharynx runs between which two points?
questions.why: The laryngopharynx serves both respiration and digestion, extending from the epiglottis to the top of the esophagus.

options.t: The soft palate and the epiglottis
options.why: That span is the oropharynx.

options.t: The vocal cords and the carina
options.why: That region is the trachea.

options.t: The nasal cavity and soft palate
options.why: That span is the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: What does the epiglottis do?
questions.why: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap protecting the tracheal opening from ingested material. It also forms the superior border of the glottis.

options.why: The vocal cords produce sound.

options.t: Separates the pharynx from the esophagus
options.why: The esophagus opens directly off the laryngopharynx.

options.t: Holds the trachea open during inhalation
options.why: Cartilage rings keep the trachea open.

options.t: Shields the trachea from swallowed material

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the three purposes of the larynx?
questions.why: The larynx joins pharynx to trachea and serves three purposes: air passage, sphincter protection, and speech. Humidifying is done by the nasal passages.

options.why: Sphincter action keeps solids and liquids out of the lungs.
Speech production is the third stated purpose.
Air passage is one of the three stated purposes.

questions.stem: Why do the arytenoid cartilages matter clinically?
questions.why: The arytenoid cartilages form the posterior attachment of the vocal cords, making them valuable guides for endotracheal intubation.

options.t: They anchor the epiglottis to the hyoid
options.why: That is a separate ligamentous attachment.
Surfactant comes from type II pneumocytes.

options.t: They form the anterior tracheal wall
options.why: They sit posteriorly, not anteriorly.

questions.stem: Which structure is part of the lower airway?
questions.why: The lower airway consists of the trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli, and lungs — everything below the glottis.

options.why: The nasal cavity is where the upper airway begins.
The oropharynx is an upper airway structure.
The larynx sits at the dividing line, in the upper airway.

questions.stem: At which landmark does the trachea split into the mainstem bronchi?
questions.why: The trachea lies anterior to the esophagus and bifurcates into the right and left primary bronchi at the carina.

options.why: The hilum is where vessels enter the lung.
The apex is the top of the lung.
The glottis is the vocal cord opening, far above.

questions.stem: Which cells produce the mucus lining the conducting airways?
questions.why: The trachea is lined with columnar epithelial tissue and goblet cells that produce the mucus blanketing the conducting airways, which is then swallowed or expectorated.

options.why: Cilia move the mucus rather than produce it.
Type II cells make surfactant, not mucus.
Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface.

questions.stem: At roughly which vertebral level do the primary bronchi branch?
questions.why: The bronchial tree begins with the right and left primary bronchi near the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra.

options.why: That is higher than the actual branch point.
That is well below the diaphragm.
That is at the base of the neck.

questions.stem: What structurally distinguishes bronchi from bronchioles?
questions.why: Bronchi possess cartilage up to about the 10th generation. Bronchioles, beginning around the 11th, lack it.

options.t: Bronchi have cartilage; bronchioles do not
Bronchi have cilia; bronchioles do not
options.why: Both are ciliated through much of their length.

options.t: Bronchi carry air; bronchioles exchange gas
options.why: Conducting bronchioles do not exchange gas either.

options.t: Bronchi are paired; bronchioles are not
options.why: Both branch extensively on each side.

questions.stem: In the airway generation system, what is generation zero?
questions.why: Generation zero is the trachea; the first-generation airways are the right and left primary bronchi.

options.why: Those are the first-generation airways.
Those sit far down the branching sequence.
Those are generations 20 to 22.

questions.stem: Where do the conducting airways end?
questions.why: Conducting airways move air toward the exchange surfaces. They begin at the nose and lips and end at the terminal bronchioles.

options.why: Those are near the start of the conducting zone.
Those are the exchange surface itself.
Those belong to the respiratory zone.

questions.stem: Which structures form the gas-exchanging units of the lungs?
questions.why: The respiratory units are the respiratory bronchioles, the alveolar ducts, and the alveoli — generations 17 through 23.

options.why: Those drive ventilation mechanically.
Those are conducting structures only.
Both belong to the conducting zone.

questions.stem: Where precisely does blood-gas exchange occur?
questions.why: Respiratory exchange between lung and blood occurs in the alveoli at the alveolocapillary membrane.

options.why: Terminal bronchioles have no alveoli.
The carina is a branching landmark.
The pleura is a covering, not an exchange surface.

questions.stem: What is distinctive about type I alveolar cells?
questions.why: Type I pneumocytes are almost empty, which allows better gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes make new type I cells and produce surfactant.

options.why: Surfactant is made by type II cells.

options.t: They can regenerate other alveolar cells
options.why: Regeneration is a type II cell capability.

options.t: They secrete mucus onto the alveolar surface
options.why: Alveoli are not mucus-producing surfaces.

options.t: They are almost empty, easing gas exchange

questions.stem: What does surfactant do?
questions.why: Surfactant from type II pneumocytes reduces surface tension and helps keep the alveoli expanded, which is what facilitates gas exchange.

options.t: Raises surface tension to aid recoil
options.why: Surfactant reduces tension rather than raising it.

options.t: Traps particles so they can be coughed up
options.why: That is the role of airway mucus.

options.t: Binds oxygen for transport across the membrane
options.why: Hemoglobin binds oxygen.

options.t: Lowers surface tension to keep alveoli open

questions.stem: How many lobes does the left lung have, and why?
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, the left being smaller to accommodate the heart.

options.t: Three, because the diaphragm rises higher
options.why: The right hemidiaphragm sits higher, and the right lung still has three.

options.t: Two, because the heart occupies space
Two, because the aorta arches over it
options.why: The heart, not the aorta, accounts for the difference.
The left lung is smaller than the right, not equal.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between visceral and parietal pleura?
questions.why: The visceral pleura covers the lungs and folds back to become the parietal pleura. Normally the two sit close together with no space between them.

options.why: The parietal layer lines the cavity wall.

options.t: Parietal covers the lung and folds back
options.why: This reverses the two layers.

options.t: Visceral covers the lung and folds back
They are permanently separated by fluid
options.why: Normally the two membranes sit together with no space.

questions.stem: Why is the pleural space called a potential space?
questions.why: The pleural space is a potential space created between the layers by disease or trauma, where fluid, air, or blood may accumulate.

options.t: None exists until disease or trauma creates it
It is a fixed cavity holding lubricating fluid
options.why: There is no fixed cavity in the healthy state.
It is not created by the breathing cycle.

options.t: It fills with air during normal breathing
options.why: Air in that space is abnormal — a pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Which vessels supply the lung tissue itself?
questions.why: Deoxygenated blood arrives via the pulmonary arteries to be oxygenated, while the bronchial arteries branch off the thoracic aorta to feed the lung tissue itself.

options.why: Those return oxygenated blood to the heart.
Those supply the heart muscle.
Those deliver blood to be oxygenated, not to feed lung tissue.

questions.stem: What is tidal volume?
questions.why: Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in a single ordinary breath.

options.t: Maximum air that can be exhaled
options.why: That describes vital capacity components.

options.t: Air moved in a single breath
Air moved in one full minute
options.why: That is minute volume.

options.t: Air left in the lungs after exhaling
options.why: That is residual volume.

questions.stem: What is inspiratory reserve volume?
questions.why: Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional air that can be inhaled after normal tidal volume has been reached.

options.t: Extra air exhaled beyond a normal breath
options.why: That is expiratory reserve volume.

options.t: Total air moved in maximal effort
options.why: That is vital capacity.

options.t: The air left in the lungs after a maximal exhalation
options.why: That is residual volume — it cannot be exhaled at all, so it is not a reserve you can draw on.

options.t: Extra air inhaled beyond a normal breath

questions.stem: What does residual volume prevent?
questions.why: Residual volume is the air remaining after maximal exhalation. It keeps alveoli slightly inflated, preventing collapse.

options.why: Aspiration is prevented by the epiglottis.
CO2 clearance depends on minute volume.
The Hering-Breuer reflex guards against overinflation.

questions.stem: Which is an example of anatomic dead space?
questions.why: Anatomic dead space is the part of the system with no alveoli — mouth, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles. Physiologic dead space is damaged alveoli that cannot exchange gas.

options.why: That is also physiologic rather than anatomic.
Capillaries are part of the exchange surface.
Damaged alveoli are physiologic dead space.

questions.stem: How is minute volume calculated?
questions.why: Minute volume is respiratory rate times tidal volume — one of the critical determinants of effective ventilation, which is why a fast shallow rate can still be inadequate.

options.why: Vital capacity is a maximal-effort measure.
Residual volume never leaves the lungs.

options.t: Respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume
Tidal volume divided by respiratory rate
options.why: Dividing gives no meaningful ventilation figure.

questions.stem: What is ventilation?
questions.why: Ventilation is the mechanical process of moving air in and out of the lungs. Its two phases together form a respiratory cycle.

options.t: Mechanically moving air in and out
Regulating blood pH via the lungs
options.why: That is one function of ventilation, not its definition.

options.t: Delivering oxygen from alveoli to tissue
options.why: That is oxygenation.

options.t: Exchanging gas between blood and tissue
options.why: That is internal respiration.

questions.stem: Which nerves innervate the diaphragm?
questions.why: The phrenic nerves arise from C3 to C5 — C3, 4, and 5 keep the diaphragm alive, which is why high cervical injury stops breathing.

options.t: The phrenic nerves, from C3 to C5
The intercostal nerves, from T1 to T12
options.why: Those supply the chest wall muscles.

options.t: The accessory nerves, from C1 to C3
options.why: The accessory nerve supplies neck muscles.

options.t: The vagus nerves, from the medulla
options.why: The vagus supplies thoracic and abdominal organs.

questions.stem: Why is the diaphragm unusual among muscles?
questions.why: The diaphragm acts as a voluntary skeletal muscle when you deliberately breathe deep or hold your breath, and as an involuntary muscle under brainstem control when CO2 rises.

options.t: It contracts without any nerve supply
options.why: It depends entirely on the phrenic nerves.

options.t: It is the only smooth muscle in the chest
options.why: It is a skeletal muscle by structure.

options.t: It holds a resting tone that keeps the chest partly expanded
options.why: The diaphragm relaxes fully with every exhalation; what makes it unusual is the dual voluntary and automatic control.

options.t: It works both voluntarily and automatically

questions.stem: Where does the diaphragm attach posteriorly?
questions.why: The diaphragm attaches to the sternum anteriorly, the ribs laterally, and the vertebrae posteriorly.

options.why: The sternum is its anterior attachment.
The scapulae are shoulder bones with no diaphragm attachment.
The ribs are its lateral attachment.

questions.stem: What does Boyle's law state?
questions.why: Boyle's law says pressure is inversely proportional to volume — expand the thorax and pressure inside drops, which is what draws air in.

options.t: Total pressure equals the sum of partials
options.why: That is Dalton's principle of partial pressures.

options.t: Gas pressure varies directly with volume
options.why: The relationship is inverse, not direct.

options.t: Gas pressure varies inversely with volume
Dissolved gas falls as pressure falls
options.why: That is Henry's law.

questions.stem: During inhalation, what happens to the diaphragm and ribs?
questions.why: Contraction drives the diaphragm down and the ribs up and out, enlarging the thoracic cavity and dropping the pressure inside so air rushes in.

options.t: Diaphragm moves up, ribs move down and in
options.why: That describes exhalation.

options.t: Diaphragm moves down, ribs move up and out
Diaphragm moves down, ribs move down and in
options.why: The rib movement is reversed here.

options.t: Diaphragm moves up, ribs move up and out
options.why: The diaphragm descends during inhalation.

questions.stem: Why is normal breathing called negative pressure ventilation?
questions.why: Negative pressure ventilation means air flows from higher pressure outside the body to lower pressure inside the lungs.

options.why: The diaphragm creates a vacuum rather than pushing.

options.t: Lung pressure falls below outside pressure
The pleural space holds negative pressure
options.why: That is true but is not what the term describes.

options.t: Lung pressure rises above outside pressure
options.why: Rising internal pressure drives exhalation.

questions.stem: How is normal exhalation characterized?
questions.why: Exhalation is passive and requires no muscular effort. It ends when intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric pressure.

options.why: Muscular effort is only needed for forced exhalation.
Diaphragm contraction produces inhalation.

options.t: Active, driven by the accessory muscles
options.why: Accessory muscles assist only when demand is high.

questions.stem: When are the accessory muscles of breathing active?
questions.why: Accessory muscles are inactive during quiet breathing. Their use signals increased work of breathing — which is why it is a distress sign.

options.t: Only when the diaphragm is paralyzed
options.why: They assist in many conditions, not just paralysis.

options.t: When demand rises, as in exercise

options.why: They are not active during quiet breathing.
Exhalation is passive and needs no assistance.

questions.stem: Which statement about ventilation and oxygenation is correct?
questions.why: Oxygenation cannot occur without ventilation, but ventilation without oxygenation happens in oxygen-depleted spaces, with carbon monoxide, or at altitude.

options.why: Oxygenation always requires ventilation first.

options.t: Neither can occur without the other
options.why: Each depends on the other in one direction only.
They are distinct processes.

questions.stem: What is the normal fraction of inspired oxygen in room air?
questions.why: FiO2 is the percentage of oxygen in inhaled air, normally 21%.

options.why: That is roughly the carbon dioxide fraction.
That is the nitrogen fraction.
That is the percentage of oxygen carried on hemoglobin.

questions.stem: External respiration occurs between which two?
questions.why: External (pulmonary) respiration is the exchange between the alveoli and the RBCs travelling through the pulmonary capillaries.

options.why: That is cellular metabolism.
That is simply air movement into the body.
That is internal respiration.

questions.stem: What total pressure does inspired air exert at sea level?
questions.why: Inspired air is roughly 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, exerting a total pressure of 760 mm Hg at sea level.

options.why: That is above atmospheric pressure at sea level.
That is closer to arterial oxygen tension.
That is below atmospheric pressure at sea level.

questions.stem: What accumulates when internal respiration lacks oxygen?
questions.why: Without adequate oxygen, cells cannot fully convert glucose to energy and lactic acid and other toxins build up. Glycolysis proceeds without oxygen but yields far less ATP.

options.why: Neither is produced by cellular metabolism.
Those are products of buffering, not oxygen debt.
Those are airway products, unrelated to metabolism.

questions.stem: What does Henry's law describe?
questions.why: Henry's law governs partial pressure: as the pressure of a gas over a liquid decreases, the amount dissolved in that liquid also decreases.

options.why: That is Boyle's law.

options.t: Dissolved gas falls as pressure falls

options.why: That is Charles's law.

options.t: Gas moves from low to high concentration
options.why: Diffusion moves down a gradient, not up it.

questions.stem: In returning venous blood, which is true of the partial pressures?
questions.why: Returning venous blood has low pO2 and high pCO2. In the lungs the reverse holds, so oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out.

options.t: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.why: That describes blood inside the lungs.

options.t: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide
Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are high
options.why: Venous blood has given up its oxygen.

options.t: Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are low
options.why: Venous blood is carrying CO2 back for removal.

questions.stem: What percentage of oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin?
questions.why: Oxygen diffuses into arterial blood where 97% combines with the hemoglobin molecule for transport.

options.why: That is the nitrogen content of air.
That understates hemoglobin's carrying role.
That is the oxygen percentage of inspired air.

questions.stem: Why do oxygen and carbon dioxide not compete for binding sites?
questions.why: Carbon dioxide has three available transport methods in venous blood while oxygen relies on hemoglobin, so the two never compete for the same sites.

options.t: Carbon dioxide has three transport methods
They are carried in different blood cells
options.why: Both travel in the same blood.
The reason is CO2's alternate routes, not reserved sites.

options.t: Carbon dioxide binds only when oxygen is low
options.why: CO2 transport does not depend on oxygen levels.

questions.stem: Ventilation is regulated primarily by what?
questions.why: Regulation is driven primarily by CSF pH, which is directly related to the carbon dioxide dissolved in blood plasma. High CO2 means acidotic.

options.t: The stretch of the alveolar walls
options.why: Stretch triggers a protective reflex, not routine control.

options.t: The oxygen saturation of arterial blood
options.why: Oxygen becomes the driver only in end-stage COPD.
Temperature influences rate but does not regulate it.

options.t: The pH of the cerebrospinal fluid

questions.stem: Which are the three components of the breathing control system?
questions.why: The control center sits in the brainstem, the effectors are the respiratory muscles, and the sensors measure CO2, pH, lung stretch, temperature, and irritants.

options.why: Those are all effectors, only one component.
The cerebellum is not part of respiratory control.
Those are all sensor types, only one component.

questions.stem: Which group can cause either inspiration or expiration?
questions.why: The ventral respiratory group in the medulla can cause inspiration or expiration depending on which motor neurons are stimulated.

options.why: That group acts as an integration center.
That center maintains consciousness.
That group smooths transitions between phases.

questions.stem: What is the role of the pontine respiratory group?
questions.why: The pontine group communicates with both the ventral and dorsal groups, smoothing the transition between each phase of the ventilatory cycle.

options.why: The phrenic nerve carries that signal.
Lung mechanoreceptors trigger that reflex.

options.t: Measuring carbon dioxide in the CSF
options.why: Central chemoreceptors do the measuring.

questions.stem: Where are the central chemoreceptors located?
questions.why: Central chemoreceptors sit in the medulla and respond to carbon dioxide and CSF pH. Peripheral ones in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to PO2, PCO2, and pH.

options.why: Those hold peripheral chemoreceptors.
Those also hold peripheral chemoreceptors.
Those contain mechanoreceptors.

questions.stem: What does carbon dioxide form after crossing into the brain?
questions.why: CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and bicarbonate, dropping pH. Chemoreceptors then drive rate and depth up to blow off CO2.

options.why: Lactic acid comes from anaerobic metabolism.
Bicarbonate is a product of dissociation, and pH falls.
Urea comes from protein metabolism in the liver.

questions.stem: In hypoxic drive, what triggers breathing?
questions.why: COPD patients retain CO2 and live at a more acidic baseline. In end-stage disease the body switches to the hypoxic drive, stimulating breathing when arterial oxygen falls.

options.why: Blood pressure is not a respiratory trigger.

options.t: A rise in arterial carbon dioxide
options.why: That is the normal trigger the patient has lost.

options.t: A rise in cerebrospinal fluid pH
options.why: Rising pH would slow breathing, not stimulate it.

questions.stem: Which reflex prevents the lungs from overinflating?
questions.why: Mechanoreceptors in the bronchi, bronchioles, and visceral pleura fire when the lungs inflate, signalling via the vagus nerves to inhibit inspiration.

options.why: That prevents aspiration.
That clears irritants from the airway.
That is a bladder reflex.

questions.stem: What do irritant receptors trigger when stimulated?
questions.why: Irritant receptors in the airway mucosa respond to smoke, pollen, dust, mucus, fumes, and cold air, triggering coughing, bronchoconstriction, or shallow breathing.

options.why: The response narrows rather than opens the airway.
That is the Hering-Breuer response.
Surfactant output is not reflex-controlled.

questions.stem: Which are the three buffer systems?
questions.why: The three are the circulating bicarbonate buffer, the respiratory system, and the renal system.

options.why: The liver is not one of the three named.
Those are chemical buffers, not the three systems named here.
The spleen has no buffering role.

questions.stem: In the bicarbonate buffer, what does excess acid become?
questions.why: Excess H+ binds bicarbonate to form carbonic acid, which breaks into water and carbon dioxide so the CO2 can simply be exhaled.

options.t: Urea, then excreted by the kidney
options.why: Urea comes from protein breakdown.

options.t: Carbonic acid, then water and CO2
Lactic acid, then stored in muscle
options.why: Lactic acid comes from anaerobic metabolism.
Bilirubin comes from red cell breakdown.

questions.stem: How quickly does the renal buffer component act?
questions.why: Raising respiratory rate is the fastest route to shedding excess H+. The kidneys monitor H+ and bicarbonate in the nephron tubules, but that takes hours or days.

options.why: That is closer to the respiratory response.
That is closer to the bicarbonate buffer's speed.
The respiratory system is considerably faster.

questions.stem: Which factor DECREASES the ventilatory rate?
questions.why: Fever, CNS stimulants, pain, emotion, hypoxia, and acidosis raise the rate. Sleep, decreased metabolic states, and CNS depressants including alcohol lower it.

options.why: Fever raises the rate.
Both drive the rate up.
Both drive the rate up.

questions.stem: Match each airway structure to its description.
questions.why: Top to bottom through the airway. The glottis is the dividing line between upper and lower, and the alveoli are where the actual work happens.
pairs: Passageway for air only; contains the turbinates
Passageway for both air and food; gag reflex site

pairs: Air moved in a single breath
Additional air that can be inhaled after normal tidal volume
Additional air that can be exhaled after tidal volume is expelled

pairs: In the medulla; respond to CO2 and CSF pH
